106.title: Варіант 1 · Завдання 6–10
106.text:
A Voice for Grandma

When seventeen-year-old Daryna Melnyk moved with her family from Kharkiv to a small town near Lviv, she found herself spending long evenings alone. Her new classmates were friendly, but she missed her grandmother, who had stayed behind and now lived on her own. Every night Daryna called her, and every night the conversation ended the same way: her grandmother complained that her eyesight was getting worse and she could no longer read the novels she loved.

That gave Daryna an idea. She began recording herself reading a chapter of a book each evening and sending the audio file to her grandmother. Within a month, her grandmother's neighbours were asking for copies. "I realised that there were thousands of people like my grandmother," Daryna says. "They didn't need expensive technology. They just needed a voice."

With the help of her computer science teacher, Daryna built a simple website where volunteers could upload recordings of Ukrainian and foreign books, and listeners could choose what they wanted to hear. At first, only her classmates took part. Then a local radio station mentioned the project, and the number of volunteers grew from twelve to more than four hundred in just six weeks.

Not everything went smoothly. Some recordings were of poor quality, and others contained mistakes. Instead of rejecting them, Daryna organised online workshops where professional actors taught volunteers how to breathe correctly, how to read dialogues and how to avoid background noise. "The workshops turned out to be the best part," she admits. "People came to help others, but they also learnt something for themselves."

Today the library contains over two thousand audiobooks, and it is used in care homes, hospitals and schools for children with visual impairments. Daryna, who is now studying journalism, still records one chapter every week. Her grandmother, she says, remains her strictest critic: "If I read too fast, she calls me the next morning to tell me!"

117.title: Варіант 1 · Завдання 17–22

Why Do We Put Things Off?

Almost everyone has put off an important task at least once. Psychologists say that procrastination is not simply laziness, (17) ____. When a task seems boring, difficult or frightening, our brain looks for a quick way to feel better, (18) ____.

The problem is that the relief does not last long. As the deadline gets closer, stress grows, (19) ____. Many students know this cycle well: they promise to start revising on Monday, then on Wednesday, and finally find themselves studying all night before the exam.

Fortunately, there are simple techniques (20) ____. One of the most popular is the "two-minute rule": if something takes less than two minutes, do it immediately. Another is to divide a big task into small steps, (21) ____.

Experts also recommend removing distractions. Putting your phone in another room, for example, can make a surprising difference. Finally, it is important to be kind to yourself, (22) ____.

A so that each one feels easy to begin
B which was invented by a famous scientist
C but a way of avoiding unpleasant emotions
D because people who blame themselves too much tend to procrastinate even more
E such as checking social media or watching a video
F although most teachers never give homework
G that can help break this habit
H and the quality of our work often suffers

206.title: Варіант 2 · Завдання 6–10
206.text:
The Village That Learned to Code

Ten years ago, Petro Kovalenko had a well-paid job at an IT company in Kyiv. He lived in a modern flat, travelled abroad for conferences and, by most people's standards, had a successful life. Yet every time he visited his parents in a small village in the Poltava region, he felt that something was missing.

"The children there were just as clever as the kids in the capital," he remembers, "but they had far fewer opportunities. The nearest computer club was forty kilometres away." In 2021, after the pandemic had shown that he could work from anywhere, Petro decided to move back home.

At first, he simply invited a few neighbours' children to his house on Saturday mornings and showed them how to build simple games. Word spread quickly. Within three months, so many children wanted to come that his living room was no longer big enough. The village council offered him an empty room in the old school building, and local businesses donated second-hand laptops.

Petro's teaching method is unusual. There are no marks and no lectures. Each student chooses a real problem in the village and tries to solve it with technology. One group created an app that tells farmers when to water their fields; another built a website for the local museum, which had never had one. "When children see that their work is useful, they don't need to be pushed," Petro explains.

The results have surprised everyone. Several of his former students are now studying computer science at universities in Kharkiv and Lviv, and two have already found part-time jobs as developers. Yet Petro insists that careers are not the main goal. "I don't want to turn every child into a programmer," he says. "I want them to believe that they can change the place where they live."

The Story of the Vyshyvanka

The vyshyvanka, the traditional embroidered shirt, is one of the best-known symbols of Ukraine. In the past, every region had its own patterns and colours, (17) ____. For example, shirts from Poltava were often decorated with white thread on white fabric, (18) ____.

Embroidery was not only decoration. People believed that certain symbols protected the person (19) ____. That is why mothers often embroidered shirts for their children by hand, spending many evenings on a single piece.

In the twentieth century, the tradition almost disappeared in big cities, (20) ____. However, since 2006 Ukrainians have celebrated Vyshyvanka Day every May, (21) ____. On this day, people wear embroidered clothes to school, to work and even on the underground.

Today, modern designers combine traditional patterns with contemporary styles, (22) ____.

A and their collections are shown at international fashion weeks
B who wore the shirt
C because cotton was too expensive for most families
D so an expert could tell where a shirt came from
E although it survived in many villages

G while those from the Carpathians were full of bright colours
